object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Identified by account number.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six digit sequential unique identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold to customers, identified by product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact - says what the customer pays and how often. Identified by plan code.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets - the feature bundle (seats, API, SSO). Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Name of a feature bundle, unique.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. / Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a certain amount on a cycle for a product/plan. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.
Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional for open-ended subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: Billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual. / Only those two.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: Status of subscription: trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with effective date and requester. Identified by change ID.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: Date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: The term 'plan' is used for three distinct concepts: the billing artefact (PricePlan), the feature bundle (FeatureBundle), and a sales-negotiated deal mentioned by Tom. The sales 'deal' concept is not modeled here since it was explicitly deferred to another meeting -- should it be included in this model?

source_references.excerpt: We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: PricePlan's identifier is described as 'plan code' but no explicit uniqueness/format confirmation was given the way AccountNumber or SubscriptionId received; confirm PlanCode is guaranteed unique and mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often.

ambiguities.description: The 'paused' flag on Subscription overlaps confusingly with the four-value status (a paused subscription can still show as 'active' status). Should Paused be modeled as a separate boolean attribute of Subscription, and if so, what are its interaction rules with status (e.g., can a cancelled subscription be paused)? The transcript flags this as a known source of bugs but doesn't resolve it, so it has been omitted from the model as an attribute pending clarification.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. / Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. / It behaves like a status. / It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

ambiguities.description: MRR is explicitly derived (from price plan and billing period) and not stored, per facilitator's decision -- it has been excluded from the model as a fact type/attribute. Confirm this exclusion is acceptable for reporting/documentation purposes, or whether a derived rule/formula should be documented explicitly in the model.

source_references.excerpt: So it's derived from the price plan and the billing period. / Derived. Yes. ... / I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run-to-term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. The model only captures the current system behaviour (end date set to paid-through date), not any refund/credit concept, since none exists in the system today. This is a known gap requiring a business/legal decision.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a rule today that I could write down? ... cancellation on an annual subscription sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues. There's no refund mechanism at all... / What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term ... is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The Subscription entity has both a denormalised 'current price plan' (part of the core Subscription record, maintained by the change process) and a full change history via PlanChange records; if the two disagree, the change history is authoritative and the current plan value is considered a bug. This creates a redundancy that is intentionally tolerated but could be seen as a derived/denormalised attribute duplicating information from PlanChange -- should 'current PricePlan' be modeled as a stored (denormalised) attribute, or purely derived from PlanChange history, for consistency with how MRR was treated?

source_references.excerpt: It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. / No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. ... it's maintained by the change process, nobody sets it by hand. / And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Account identification: Tom notes that when an account closes and the same company returns, they receive a new account number, so the same real-world company can map to multiple Account records over time. Is 'Company' a distinct concept from 'Account' that should be modeled separately, or is this intentionally out of scope since the business treats each account number as a wholly new customer?

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. / Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' but not yet defined or confirmed as identified by product code; the value constraint on ProductCode (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) may need revisiting once the fourth product is finalized.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.
